# How To Improve Your CIBIL Score In India In 10 Steps

A poor CIBIL score can affect your ability to borrow. This can be anything from credit cards to personal loans and mortgages. However, your CIBIL score isn’t set in stone and you can improve it over time by being responsible with your borrowing.

There isn’t a quick way to Improve Your score. Instead, learn what’s on your report, what the problem areas are and work on improving your habits. This guide will give you some realistic ways to Improve Your CIBIL score in India. It won’t guarantee you’ll get approved for a loan and you shouldn’t take any personal credit advice.

## What Is A CIBIL Score?

A CIBIL score is a 3 digit score which summarises your credit history. This is based on your Credit Information Report (CIR). It will generally range between 300 and 900. Lenders can use this alongside your income, existing EMIs and their own lending criteria.

The report will show information about your credit accounts including any loans or credit cards. However, it won’t include any savings, fixed deposits or investments. A high score can mean you’re better with your credit but doesn’t guarantee you’ll get approved for a loan.

## What Is A Good CIBIL Score?

Scores of 700+ are generally considered a good score according to CIBIL. Lenders will have their own criteria for what they consider a good score and this can vary depending on the product and applicant. A score closer to 900 can help boost your profile.

However, if you have a score of below 700, then it’s a good idea to look at your report before applying again. You may have missed payments, high credit card balances, too many applications, a short credit history or errors.

## 10 Ways To Improve Your CIBIL Score

### 1. Pay All EMIs And Credit Card Bills On Time

Your payment history is an important part of your credit profile. If you don’t pay on time, lenders may see you as a higher risk. Try setting reminders a few days before your due dates. If you’re using auto debit, make sure you’ve got enough money in your account linked. You can also check that your payment went through.

Wherever possible try to pay the full amount on your credit card. Whilst paying the minimum can prevent you from having a missed payment, the balance can accrue interest.

### 2. Keep Credit Card Utilisation Low

Credit utilisation shows how much of your available limit you’re using. For example if you have a credit card with a limit of ₹1,00,000 and your balance is ₹70,000 then you’re using 70% of your available limit. High utilisation can suggest you’re reliant on your credit.

Try to keep your balances well below your limit. It’s commonly suggested to keep it under 30% however this isn’t a guaranteed CIBIL score. If you can, try to pay some of your balance before your statement date. Don’t overspend as your limit is increased.

### 3. Don’t Apply for Too Many Loans or Cards

When you apply for credit with a lender, they may perform a hard search. If you’re applying for multiple credits in a short space of time, you’ll have multiple searches.

Before applying compare the eligibility, costs and terms of your loan. Only use eligibility tools if you know whether this will be a soft or hard search. Only apply if you really need it.

### 4. Check Your CIBIL Report Regularly

Your report will show whether you have any overdue amounts, unknown accounts, incorrect information and searches. CIBIL will give you one free CIBIL Score and Report per year through the official site.

Check that your report shows any closed loans are correct, that the balances look correct and that payments are being recorded correctly. Keep any receipts, statements and loan closure letters. Start here to get your [free CIBIL score and report](https://www.cibil.com/freecibilscore).

### 5. Dispute Any Errors

Your report may show incorrect overdue amounts, loans you didn’t take out, duplicate accounts or payments which haven’t been updated. Dispute this with CIBIL and get in touch with the lender who provided the information.

CIBIL generally aren’t able to change the data provided by lenders. The credit institution will need to verify and approve any corrections. Provide any evidence and note down the reference number. Don’t pay any agents who promise to wipe correct negative information.

### 6. Pay Off Balances Strategically

Create a realistic repayment plan to pay off your balances. Pay the required amount by your due dates and if possible pay extra to balances which are expensive. If your account is overdue, get in touch with the lender through their official channels to confirm the amount, charges and options.

Don’t take on a new loan with high interest rates to Improve Your score. If you’re unable to pay the full amount, get in touch with the lender. Get any changes in writing and ensure you have proof of payment.

### 7. Be Responsible With Older Accounts

Having older accounts can help with your profile. If you have an older account with a consistent repayment history then this can show you have experience with credit.

Don’t close any older cards which you’ve been responsible with. Check the annual fee and terms first. If you keep it, make sure you’re using it within your budget and paying on time. Never keep a card which is expensive or not suitable just to Improve Your score.

### 8. Have A Healthy Credit Mix

Your report could have secured credit, such as a mortgage or vehicle loan. Or it could have unsecured credit, such as personal loans or credit cards. CIBIL advise to have a healthy mix but don’t take on too many unsecured loans.

Don’t take on credit just to create a mix. Only take on credit for a genuine reason and ensure you can afford to repay. If you don’t have a loan, don’t assume you need a personal loan to Improve Your score.

### 9. Be Responsible With Joint Accounts

If you’re missing payments on a joint, co-signed or guaranteed loan this can affect your credit history. Just because someone else is paying your monthly payment doesn’t mean they’re solely responsible.

Regularly check these accounts and get in touch before your due dates. If you’re a guarantor, make sure you understand what you’ve committed to.

### 10. Allow Time for Changes

Improving your credit habits and updating your report isn’t an instant process. Lenders will report information to the credit bureaux periodically. This means it could take some time for your payments or corrections to show. CIBIL state that it typically takes around 15-30 days for updates but can vary.

Continue to pay on time, keep your utilisation low and Check Your report after a reasonable amount of time. There isn’t a set time frame as it depends on your full credit history.

## How Long Does It Take To Improve My CIBIL Score?

There isn’t a set time frame. If you’ve recently had a payment reported it could show once the lender has updated the information. If you’ve had repeated late payments or a serious default it could take longer to improve. You’ll need to have a good repayment history.

Disputes can take around 30 days depending on the response from the credit institution. Keep track of your dispute. Just because you’ve requested it doesn’t mean it’ll show straight away. Beware of any services which promise to Improve Your score by a set amount in 30 days.

## Common Mistakes Which Can Affect Your CIBIL Score

- Missing payments on your EMIs.
- Using most of your available credit.
- Applying for multiple loans/cards in a short space of time.
- Ignoring entries on your report as you think your loan should be gone.
- Guaranteeing without keeping track of repayments.
- Paying an agent to Improve Your score by removing correct defaults.
- Taking on unnecessary loans to create a mix.

Instead try to Check Your report, keep a repayment schedule and only borrow when you understand the cost.

## How To Check Your CIBIL Score For Free

Go to the [official CIBIL site](https://www.cibil.com/freecibilscore). Choose the free CIBIL Score and Report option and register. You’ll need to verify your identity. CIBIL will give you one free score and report per year. Ensure you’re using the official site and don’t give any sensitive information such as your PAN, OTP, password etc. to unknown callers or links.

Once you’ve received your report Check Your personal details, account details, payment history, balances and search section. Save a copy of your report either by downloading or securely storing it. If you spot any discrepancies, dispute this through the official CIBIL process and get in touch with your lender.

## FAQs: How To Improve Your CIBIL Score

### 1. How Can I Improve My CIBIL Score Quickly?

Start by paying all of your current dues on time, pay down any high credit card balances and don’t apply unnecessarily. Check Your report for any errors and dispute any incorrect information. There’s no guaranteed quick fix. Improvements will depend on your credit history and how quickly lenders report updated information.

### 2. Can I Improve My CIBIL Score In 30 Days?

Some updates can show within 15-30 days once the lender has reported. However this doesn’t mean everyone’s score will improve within 30 days. If you have long standing late payments or defaults this may take longer to improve.

### 3. Does Checking My Own CIBIL Score Affect It?

Checking your own score through CIBIL is a self check. When you apply for a loan or credit card with a lender they will carry out a search. Regularly Check Your report and don’t apply unnecessarily.

### 4. What’s The Fastest Way To Improve My CIBIL Score From 600 To 750?

There isn’t a set way or time frame to Improve Your score from 600 to 750. Look at your report and identify why your score is low. Where possible pay down overdue amounts, keep your card utilisation low, dispute any errors and ensure you’re paying on time. This will depend on the details and how old the negative information is.

### 5. Does Paying The Minimum On My Credit Card Help?

Paying the minimum by your due date can help prevent you from having a missed payment. However it won’t remove the balance. You may still incur interest and high utilisation can affect your profile. It’s generally better to pay the full amount.

### 6. How Do I Correct Incorrect Loan/Payment Information?

Dispute through the official CIBIL site. Get in touch with the lender who reported the account. Provide any relevant statements, payment receipts or closure documents. CIBIL will work with the credit institution to verify. You can’t just ask for incorrect entries to be removed.

### 7. Can I Have A CIBIL Score If I’ve Never Taken Out A Loan Or Credit Card?

You may have no score or a ‘No Hit’. This is because you haven’t had enough credit activity. A credit score is based on your reported credit history. It won’t take into account your savings or salary. Don’t take on unnecessary debt to create a score.

## Final Thoughts

Improving your CIBIL score means creating a consistent history of responsible borrowing. Pay on time, keep your credit card balances low, be careful with your applications and Check Your report for any errors. Dispute any incorrect information.

Avoid any guaranteed improvements and don’t take on unnecessary debt. Allow time for updates and focus on improving your habits. Lenders will still look at your full financial situation.

Start by paying all of your current dues on time, pay down any high credit card balances and don’t apply unnecessarily. Check Your report for any errors and dispute any incorrect information. There’s no guaranteed quick fix. Improvements will depend on your credit history and how quickly lenders report updated information.

2. Can I Improve My CIBIL Score In 30 Days?

Some updates can show within 15-30 days once the lender has reported. However this doesn’t mean everyone’s score will improve within 30 days. If you have long standing late payments or defaults this may take longer to improve.

3. Does Checking My Own CIBIL Score Affect It?

Checking your own score through CIBIL is a self check. When you apply for a loan or credit card with a lender they will carry out a search. Regularly Check Your report and don’t apply unnecessarily.

4. What’s The Fastest Way To Improve My CIBIL Score From 600 To 750?

There isn’t a set way or time frame to Improve Your score from 600 to 750. Look at your report and identify why your score is low. Where possible pay down overdue amounts, keep your card utilisation low, dispute any errors and ensure you’re paying on time. This will depend on the details and how old the negative information is.

5. Does Paying The Minimum On My Credit Card Help?

Paying the minimum by your due date can help prevent you from having a missed payment. However it won’t remove the balance. You may still incur interest and high utilisation can affect your profile. It’s generally better to pay the full amount.

6. How Do I Correct Incorrect Loan/Payment Information?

Dispute through the official CIBIL site. Get in touch with the lender who reported the account. Provide any relevant statements, payment receipts or closure documents. CIBIL will work with the credit institution to verify. You can’t just ask for incorrect entries to be removed.

7. Can I Have A CIBIL Score If I’ve Never Taken Out A Loan Or Credit Card?

You may have no score or a ‘No Hit’. This is because you haven’t had enough credit activity. A credit score is based on your reported credit history. It won’t take into account your savings or salary. Don’t take on unnecessary debt to create a score.

Final Thoughts

Improving your CIBIL score means creating a consistent history of responsible borrowing. Pay on time, keep your credit card balances low, be careful with your applications and Check Your report for any errors. Dispute any incorrect information.

Avoid any guaranteed improvements and don’t take on unnecessary debt. Allow time for updates and focus on improving your habits. Lenders will still look at your full financial situation.

An introduction to India’s National Pension System, including Tier I and Tier II, contributions, investment choices, tax treatment and exit rules under current regulations.

The National Pension System (NPS) is a regulated pension saving scheme. Eligible NPS subscribers can fund a pension account and invest according to the rules in the appropriate model. The value may vary based on the investment options selected within the scheme. However, this scheme isn’t a deposit and pension doesn’t mean guaranteed returns.

As a salaried individual starting out with this scheme you’ll want to understand how your account works, what model you’re on and what limitations there are on funding and withdrawing. Retirement products can be quite complex to understand and it’s easy to get caught up with the tax benefit or balance. Other factors to consider include how easily the funds can be accessed, the risk involved with investing, fees, exit requirements, and what happens with the pension income.

## Tier I and Tier II

Tier I is the primary retirement account and withdrawals are restricted by the NPS exit and partial-withdrawal rules. Tier II is an optional investment account available to eligible subscribers who hold an active Tier I account, subject to the applicable NPS model and operational rules. Ordinary Tier II contributions do not generally receive the same tax deductions as Tier I contributions, and Tier II withdrawals are more flexible.

There is a special **Tier II Tax Saver Scheme** for eligible Central Government employees with an active Tier I account. PFRDA’s government-sector FAQs state that this option has a three-year lock-in and is not the same as an ordinary Tier II account. Do not assume this tax-saver feature applies to all subscribers or all employer models. Check the rules for your own sector and account before investing or withdrawing. [PFRDA: Government-sector NPS exit FAQs](https://www.pfrda.org.in/documents/33652/676426/Exits%2Band%2BWithdrawals%2Bunder%2BNPS%2Bfor%2BGovernment%2BSector%2B%28CG%2B%2BCAB%29.pdf).

Ensure you’re aware of any changes in the rules by checking the current PFRDA rules and official NPS resources. Sometimes this can be covered in a short article or social media post but you may be on a different model. Government employees, corporate and all citizen models will have different conditions. The exact model you’re on is a fact.

## Contributions and Investments

Your contributions will go into your NPS account and be invested according to your chosen options within the relevant model. There are various investment options available and they may have different levels of exposure to equities, corporate bonds, government securities and other acceptable assets. Each will carry different risks. Equities can be volatile, corporate bonds can be at risk of interest rates and credit risk and government securities will still have market risk as they can be sold before they mature.

Some schemes will allow you to choose your asset allocation or investment manager within certain conditions. Ensure you understand what conditions apply to your account by looking at official resources. Don’t choose an asset allocation purely because it has had higher returns in the past. This is a long term account and you won’t know the balance on the day you exit.

## Retirement Planning

Whilst calculators can show you what a large balance you’ll have after years of contributing, you’ll need to remember this is just an estimate. It won’t take into consideration inflation and how much this will really be worth. It also doesn’t guarantee the balance will be achieved. You’ll have to work with one rate of return whereas your investments will fluctuate.

When planning for your pension income you’ll need to think about how long you’ll need the money for, how much you expect to spend in your household, healthcare costs, dependants and other sources of income. The NPS is part of a wider pension and savings system so whilst you should understand what you’ll be spending in the future, this will depend on the rules of your account and the decisions you’ve made.

## Tax

For Tax Year 2026-27, the Income-tax Act, 2025 applies. Section 124 covers eligible contributions to a notified pension scheme such as NPS. In broad terms:

- An employee may claim a deduction for an eligible employer contribution, subject to a percentage-of-salary ceiling. The limit is 14% for contributions by Central or State Government employers. For other employers it is 10%, increased to 14% where the employee’s income is taxed under the default regime in section 202(1).
- An individual may claim a deduction of up to ₹50,000 for their own eligible contribution under section 124(3), subject to the conditions and the rule against claiming the same amount again under section 123.
- Eligible contributions to NPS may also fall within section 123 and Schedule XV’s aggregate ₹1.5 lakh deduction under the old regime, subject to the schedule’s conditions. Section 123 deductions are not available under the new concessional regime in section 202.

These limits are not interchangeable: employer contributions, an individual’s own contributions and contributions claimed under section 123 have separate conditions. The treatment of withdrawals and annuity income is also separate. Read [section 124 of the Income-tax Act, 2025](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/Documents/Act/Income-tax-Act-2025.pdf), [section 123](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-123-92), and the Income-tax Department’s [transition FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/81799/11848482/FAQs-on-Interplay-and-Transition.pdf/05f80c1a-073c-a5d7-fb6f-55509242be53?doAsUserId=9rMQatnoqCcGNU9mEWvVNA%3D%3D&t=1774082865717). Confirm the current rule for your employment category and tax regime before filing.

There can be tax implications based on when you exit your account. If you take a lump sum, buy an annuity and receive income from it this can be taxed differently. There may also be conditions around partial withdrawals and full exits.

## Exiting Your Account

There are rules around exiting your NPS account. This can depend on your age, why you’re exiting, what model you’re on, what balance you have and the current regulations. In some cases you’ll be required to purchase an annuity using a portion of your corpus. You’ll need to understand what the terms are and how this will be taxed.

An annuity is not the same as having liquidity. Once you’ve purchased an annuity you may have limited access to your initial capital. The amount you receive will vary depending on the product. This article isn’t recommending any annuity providers or exiting methods but explains why you should understand this part of your account before contributing for many years.

## Liquidity and Fees

Tier I accounts are intended for retirement and may have restrictions on withdrawing funds. This means they may not be suitable for holding funds which you may need to access soon. An emergency fund and short term savings are different products. If you need to access cash for medical bills or temporary employment gaps you should understand what the partial withdrawal conditions are.

You may have charges for maintaining your account, transactions and funds. Ensure you’re aware of the current charges by looking at the official schedule. Even a small charge can add up over time. Ensure you’re comparing like-for-like.

## Misconceptions

NPS doesn’t guarantee a fixed return. Not all tiers will have the same tax benefits. The balance isn’t guaranteed to be a set amount of pension. The exit rules may vary for different subscribers. This can cause you to focus on the positive aspects and ignore the limitations.

You may also delay researching the exit rules. Understanding the terms will help you understand how this can work for you in your overall plan. By reading the rules early on you’ll understand the balance between a retirement focused account and flexibility.

## Checklist

Before opening or changing your account understand what model you’re on. Ensure you’re eligible and understand how your account works. Look at your investment options, risks and fees. Ensure you understand the latest tax rules. Keep records of your contributions. If your employment has changed check if there are any corporate or employer contributions to consider.

Use the PFRDA website to understand the current regulations and subscriber guidance. Use the Income Tax Department resources to understand any tax implications. If there are specific circumstances around your exit, disability, death, employment status etc then general education may not cover all conditions.

## Summary

The NPS is a retirement focused account with investments, exit rules and tax. Tier I and Tier II aren’t interchangeable and the model you’re on can impact things. Understand the risks, limitations, fees and exit process before assuming the balance will be your pension income. This is an educational article and cannot advise you what to contribute or choose.

## Employer Contributions

Some individuals will come across NPS through their employer. How they contribute, record and are taxed may vary. Ensure you’re aware of how much has actually been contributed to your account by looking at your payslips, any communication from your employer and your account statements. If you’re receiving an employer contribution as part of your compensation understand how it will be described in your employment documents and how it will be taxed currently.

Ensure you keep records of your confirmation of contributions and annual statements. Ensure you’re aware of what you’re being paid in your payroll and what your account provider is showing. This is particularly important towards the end of a tax year. If they don’t match contact your employer or account provider via their official channels.

## Review Retirement Assumptions

Your retirement age, family commitments and expected spending can change throughout your working life. Whilst it’s a good idea to periodically review why you’re saving for retirement, don’t make a change due to short term market fluctuations. Consider the rules of your account, what assets you’re invested in, fees and how this fits into your wider household. You’re not trying to predict everything that will happen but to ensure you’re not leaving your assumption in place forever.

## Check the account details before increasing contributions

An NPS account is not just a monthly deduction. Review the subscriber details, nominee information, registered mobile number, email address, bank mandate and contribution history. If you are salaried, compare the amount shown in your payslip with the contribution reflected in the account. An employer contribution and your own contribution are not interchangeable for tax purposes, so keep the records separate. If a contribution is missing, raise it with the employer or the relevant NPS service channel and retain the acknowledgement.

Look at the investment choice and asset allocation as well. The value can move with markets, and a retirement account may contain different asset classes with different risk characteristics. Understand whether you selected an active choice or an auto choice, what the permitted allocation rules are and whether your current selection still matches your time horizon and tolerance for volatility. Do not change the allocation simply because one asset class had a strong recent year.

## Estimate retirement income cautiously

A projected corpus is not the same as a guaranteed pension. Any calculator result depends on assumptions about contribution growth, investment returns, charges, inflation and the number of years remaining. Small changes to those assumptions can produce a very different estimate. Try more than one scenario and label each one clearly. A projection using a steady return is a teaching illustration; real returns will not arrive in a straight line.

Think about the expenses the retirement corpus may need to support. Housing, healthcare, dependants and location can change the amount required. Inflation matters because the same rupee amount will buy less in the future. It may help to review the projection annually and after a salary change, but avoid treating a single target as precise. NPS can form one part of a wider retirement plan alongside EPF, PPF, other savings and any pension entitlements.

## Understand exit rules before you need the money

Old vs New Tax Regime: How Salaried People Can Compare Under Current Indian Tax Rules
Compare India’s old and new tax regimes by tax year, taxable income, eligible deductions and verified official rules, using an illustrative calculation method.
Income-tax Act, 2025 and Finance Act 2026 official tax-year guidance

To make sure you have the correct figures to compare old vs new tax regimes, you will first need to know what tax year you are looking at. From the 1st April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 will apply to tax years starting from that date. There is now no reference to previous years, it will instead be called a tax year. There could be references to previous years in relation to your returns, so whilst writing your article you need to be careful not to mix up the tax year example with any sections and rules from an old assessment year article.

Whilst the new regime is the default regime for eligible taxpayers, there could be an option to choose the old regime as a taxpayer. The new regime isn’t just “lower rates versus deductions.” You will need to calculate your taxable income and tax based on the rules of both regimes. This means you need to know:

## What year you are looking at?

If your income was earned between the 1st April 2026 and 31st March 2027, you will be in Tax Year 2026-27 based on the new act. If your income was earned in the previous financial year, you can still refer to this as Assessment Year 2026-27 based on the old act. Even though they can look similar, you must make sure you always use the correct year and act in the official calculator.

### Tax Year 2026-27: headline slab rates

For an individual below 60 years, the headline slab rates are shown below. These are marginal slab rates, not a flat rate on the whole income. Special-rate income (for example, certain capital gains), surcharge, rebate, deductions and other adjustments can change the final liability.

| Taxable income slab | Default new regime | Old regime (individual below 60) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Up to ₹2,50,000 | 0% | 0% |
| ₹2,50,001–₹4,00,000 | 0% | 5% on amount above ₹2.5 lakh |
| ₹4,00,001–₹5,00,000 | 5% | 5% on amount above ₹2.5 lakh |
| ₹5,00,001–₹8,00,000 | 5% | 20% on amount above ₹5 lakh |
| ₹8,00,001–₹10,00,000 | 10% | 20% on amount above ₹5 lakh |
| ₹10,00,001–₹12,00,000 | 10% | 30% on amount above ₹10 lakh |
| ₹12,00,001–₹16,00,000 | 15% | 30% on amount above ₹10 lakh |
| ₹16,00,001–₹20,00,000 | 20% | 30% on amount above ₹10 lakh |
| ₹20,00,001–₹24,00,000 | 25% | 30% on amount above ₹10 lakh |
| Above ₹24,00,000 | 30% | 30% on amount above ₹10 lakh |

For the default new regime, the basic exemption is ₹4 lakh. A resident individual may receive a rebate of up to ₹60,000 where total income does not exceed ₹12 lakh, subject to the law’s conditions and marginal relief just above that threshold. A standard deduction of up to ₹75,000 is available against salary/pension income under the new regime. Under the old regime, the standard deduction is ₹50,000; the rebate for a resident individual is up to ₹12,500 where total income does not exceed ₹5 lakh. The old-regime basic exemption is age-dependent: ₹2.5 lakh for individuals below 60, ₹3 lakh for resident senior citizens aged 60–79, and ₹5 lakh for resident super-senior citizens aged 80 or above.

Health and Education Cess is 4% of income tax plus surcharge. Surcharge may apply above the prescribed income thresholds and its rate/cap depends on the regime and type of income. Do not use this summary for special-rate income, non-resident cases, or a taxpayer with complex income without checking the official calculation. The new regime is the default under section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The rates and rebate above are based on the Finance Act 2026 / official tax-year guidance. [Income Tax Department: Tax Year 2026-27 rates](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/81799/11848482/memo-2026.pdf/fe530cfa-9c49-fc5c-4bfa-fc96fd5e7b7a?t=1770008674037) | [Income Tax Department: Budget 2026 FAQs](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/Documents/Budget2026/FAQs-Budget-2026.pdf).

Know what income you’re comparing.

You will need to start with the same salary and income. Salary can have multiple components and the amount you received into your bank account may not be the same amount of taxable income. You will need to know what changes to your taxable income based on your employer contributing, allowances, perquisites, interest, capital gains and other incomes. You will need to know based on the rules what to include, what is exempt and what you can deduct.

## What deductions and exemptions are eligible?

There could be some deductions and exemptions available in the old regime that aren’t available / limited in the new regime. The new regime may also have different rates and conditions. Just because you have made a payment doesn’t mean you will get a deduction. You will need to know if they are eligible based on the provision and whether there is any documentation or limits.

How to compare step-by-step.

Start by gathering the salary statement for the year, any form 16 available, other income and eligible deductions. Calculate your taxable income based on the old regime and only the deductions available. Then calculate your taxable income based on the new regime and eligible deductions and exemptions. Apply the correct rates and rebates (double checked) for the correct tax year. Compare the total tax including any cess and surcharge.

This will give you the same income and time period for both sides of the comparison. If you are making a deduction in one regime that isn’t available in the other, this won’t be a valid comparison. Using a spreadsheet can help you see how each item has affected your total. However, you should use the official calculator to double check. Keep your assumptions so you can review changes to salary components or tax rules.

Example calculation.

The Public Provident Fund (PPF) is a small savings scheme that is backed by the Government. Unlike a bank savings account your money will be invested for a long period of time and will be subject to the rules of the scheme. It is also different to a market linked mutual fund as the PPF account follows the rules of the notified scheme and therefore the interest rate can vary dependent on declaration by the Government. When researching a PPF you should look at the difference between the interest rate and the rules of the scheme.

## PPF Structure & Eligibility

This account can be opened in the name of an eligible individual either via an authorised bank or post office. The rules state who can open the account, if there can be joint names on the account, how the account operates for minors and that you cannot open more than one account in the same name. You should look at the latest official documentation for the rules of the scheme. There may be additional steps required by the banks/post offices for you to complete to ensure you meet the requirements for opening the account such as confirming your identity, nominating and making deposits.

The PPF account is designed for long term savings. You will make deposits into the account and interest will be added using the interest calculation method from the scheme. As the timing of the deposits may affect the interest, do not assume that you can make deposits on any day of the year. The latest official guidance will tell you what the calculation method is and what the timing requirements are.

## Minimum and Maximum Deposits

The official documentation for the scheme will state what the minimum deposit per year is and the maximum amount that can be contributed to the account. This should be checked to ensure the correct information is known as these are facts and could change. If you are unable to meet the minimum deposit requirement the account could be affected and there may be a process to reactivate the account and/or charges applied based on the rules. Do not rely on information from an old blog or screenshot.

Your deposits should be planned to ensure they work with your cash flow and you are not needing to borrow or ignore any immediate payments. You can choose to make a monthly deposit, however the PPF scheme may allow different deposit patterns. The timing should take into consideration your salary dates, annual costs and how much cash you have available outside of the account. The PPF is not a substitute for emergency cash.

## Length of Investment & Extending the Account

The PPF is intended to be a long term investment however there are rules in place regarding extending the account. The maturity date will impact when you can access the funds and what options you have. The process for extending the account and how any additional contributions will be dealt with should be checked against the latest official rules. Do not assume all extension options will have the same impact.

When opening an account you should consider how long the funds will be tied up for and whether this works with your reasons for opening the account. If you need the money for a deposit on a house, a business cost or school fee before the maturity date then you may need to hold funds elsewhere. Whilst having a long investment period can encourage you to save for the future it can also have less flexibility. Ensure you know what the account will be used for before making large deposits into it.

## Interest Rate Declarations

The interest rates are declared by the Government for small savings schemes for specific periods of time. The interest rate shown on the official page is a declaration for the period and is not guaranteed to be the rate for the whole life of your new account. You can be misled if you calculate using the rate for 15 years as this is an example.

Using an online calculator you should check if the calculator assumes a fixed rate. If so then this is an example. More carefully, you should note what rate was used and when it was checked. Future declarations may vary. The actual balance in the account will be based on the rules and rates.

## Withdrawing & Loans

The PPF has specific rules for when partial withdrawals can be made, how much can be withdrawn and if there is an option for loans during a specific period. The account will need to be a certain age and meet the conditions of the scheme. It is not a regular savings account and you should not assume you can withdraw at any time you need to pay for something. You should check the latest rules with the official scheme and the institution.

Having restrictions on accessing your funds can be both a positive and a negative. If you have an irregular income, dependents or high medical exposure you may want to have a separate cash fund. Having your emergency cash tied up in a long term account can cause problems with timing.

## Tax Status

For Tax Year 2026-27, eligible PPF deposits can be included in the aggregate deduction under section 123 read with Schedule XV of the Income-tax Act, 2025, up to ₹1.5 lakh across the qualifying payments listed there. This deduction is available under the old regime, subject to the schedule’s conditions; it is not available under the default new regime in section 202.

Interest credited to a PPF account and qualifying payments from the account receive the exemption provided under the PPF scheme and the applicable income-tax provisions. Do not extend that statement to every transaction without checking the account’s compliance with the scheme, the nature of the receipt and the current law. PPF’s tax treatment is often described as exempt contribution, exempt interest and exempt qualifying maturity proceeds, but the contribution deduction and the exemption on interest/withdrawal are separate legal questions.

For the contribution deduction, read [section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-123-92) and Schedule XV. For the scheme’s account and deposit conditions, read the [Public Provident Fund Scheme, 2019](https://nsiindia.gov.in/InternalPage.aspx?Id_Pk=169). Check the latest Income-tax Department guidance before filing a return.

Not all taxpayers will find it beneficial to get a tax deduction. Depending on the regime you may not be able to claim it or it may not be relevant. You should not make a contribution purely to get a tax tag on the account. You should always refer to the official Income Tax Department guidance.

## Drawbacks

The most obvious downside is the long investment period, however there are several others. The interest rate can change, the account can be restrictive and it isn’t as exposed to the market as an equity investment. Just because it is Government backed doesn’t mean it will be suitable for all purposes. When comparing to other savings you should look at the purpose and rules.

There can also be administration issues. Ensuring the details are up to date, deposits have been added to the account, keeping statements, knowing what your nominations are and ensuring any service is completed correctly. A small error when making deposits can cause problems when trying to access your funds at maturity/withdrawal. Keep records and use the official process with your institution.

## Common Misconceptions

The PPF is not a daily account. Do not assume the interest rate will stay the same for the whole investment period. Do not assume you will automatically be able to extend your account on your preferred terms. Do not assume the tax status will be the same as in an article before 2026. A long term account can be difficult to change once you have deposited your funds.

## Summary

The PPF is a long term small savings scheme with set rules on contributions, maturity and withdrawal. It may be suitable for some long term savings purposes however you should be aware of the lack of liquidity and varying interest rates. You should check the latest scheme documentation for rules, check what the conditions are for making deposits and withdrawing and check the tax status. This is an explanatory guide outlining what the account is like. Whether it is suitable for your household will depend on your circumstances.

## Administration for Long Term Account

As the account will run for a long period of time you may have moved house, changed your phone number, bank or family circumstances. Ensure your contact details are updated, check your nominations and store your account details securely. If you are moving your account between an authorised bank and post office you should follow the current official process and keep evidence of your request. Never give away your passwords, PIN or one time passwords to someone claiming to help you with an everyday update.

Before your account reaches maturity check what the official process is and what the deadline is for requesting an extension or withdrawal. Do not leave it until the last week to find out you need to fill in forms, sign and confirm your identity. The exact process can vary per institution so you should check the current written guidance.

## Consideration for Household

You should think about what your immediate cash needs are, other savings and any long term commitments. If you have a large balance in a locked account you may still struggle to pay for something unexpected if you don’t have an emergency cash fund. Some people may like having a structured long term account and intentionally keep some money separate for shorter term. Knowing what the purpose of the account is will make it clearer.

Don’t be confused by the Government backed scheme. This doesn’t mean you will get the same rate and rules in the future. The account will operate based on the legal terms and official declarations. You should double check these when making a big decision.

## Double Check Information

If you are seeing different info in your bank app, post office passbook and online calculator firstly check the dates and that all your deposits have been added. The projection may be using a fixed rate whereas your actual account will show the rate applicable for the periods. Check your transaction ledger and official interest rate declaration. If you still can’t understand why there is a difference you should contact your institution using their official process and keep your complaint reference.

You should be aware of the difference between the maximum deposit and maximum balance. If there is a maximum deposit per year based on the rules of the scheme this does not mean there is a maximum balance. The current official rules will tell you what the maximum is and what will happen if you exceed it. Do not assume based on what a calculator says or what someone else says.

## Build a contribution habit without stretching cash flow

PPF is a long-term account, so the contribution plan should be sustainable. You can deposit in one payment or in instalments, subject to the scheme's annual minimum and maximum. Before choosing a monthly amount, account for rent, EMIs, insurance premiums, school fees and emergency savings. A contribution that forces you to borrow on a credit card defeats the purpose of disciplined saving. If your income is irregular, you may prefer to make contributions when cash is available while keeping track of the annual minimum and deadline.

The most obvious downside is the long investment period, however there are several others. The interest rate can change, the account can be restrictive and it isn’t as exposed to the market as an equity investment. Just because it is Government backed doesn’t mean it will be suitable for all purposes. When comparing to other savings you should look at the purpose and rules.

There can also be administration issues. Ensuring the details are up to date, deposits have been added to the account, keeping statements, knowing what your nominations are and ensuring any service is completed correctly. A small error when making deposits can cause problems when trying to access your funds at maturity/withdrawal. Keep records and use the official process with your institution.

Common Misconceptions

The PPF is not a daily account. Do not assume the interest rate will stay the same for the whole investment period. Do not assume you will automatically be able to extend your account on your preferred terms. Do not assume the tax status will be the same as in an article before 2026. A long term account can be difficult to change once you have deposited your funds.

Summary

The PPF is a long term small savings scheme with set rules on contributions, maturity and withdrawal. It may be suitable for some long term savings purposes however you should be aware of the lack of liquidity and varying interest rates. You should check the latest scheme documentation for rules, check what the conditions are for making deposits and withdrawing and check the tax status. This is an explanatory guide outlining what the account is like. Whether it is suitable for your household will depend on your circumstances.

Administration for Long Term Account

As the account will run for a long period of time you may have moved house, changed your phone number, bank or family circumstances. Ensure your contact details are updated, check your nominations and store your account details securely. If you are moving your account between an authorised bank and post office you should follow the current official process and keep evidence of your request. Never give away your passwords, PIN or one time passwords to someone claiming to help you with an everyday update.

Before your account reaches maturity check what the official process is and what the deadline is for requesting an extension or withdrawal. Do not leave it until the last week to find out you need to fill in forms, sign and confirm your identity. The exact process can vary per institution so you should check the current written guidance.

Consideration for Household

You should think about what your immediate cash needs are, other savings and any long term commitments. If you have a large balance in a locked account you may still struggle to pay for something unexpected if you don’t have an emergency cash fund. Some people may like having a structured long term account and intentionally keep some money separate for shorter term. Knowing what the purpose of the account is will make it clearer.

Don’t be confused by the Government backed scheme. This doesn’t mean you will get the same rate and rules in the future. The account will operate based on the legal terms and official declarations. You should double check these when making a big decision.

Double Check Information

If you are seeing different info in your bank app, post office passbook and online calculator firstly check the dates and that all your deposits have been added. The projection may be using a fixed rate whereas your actual account will show the rate applicable for the periods. Check your transaction ledger and official interest rate declaration. If you still can’t understand why there is a difference you should contact your institution using their official process and keep your complaint reference.

You should be aware of the difference between the maximum deposit and maximum balance. If there is a maximum deposit per year based on the rules of the scheme this does not mean there is a maximum balance. The current official rules will tell you what the maximum is and what will happen if you exceed it. Do not assume based on what a calculator says or what someone else says.

Build a contribution habit without stretching cash flow

PPF is a long-term account, so the contribution plan should be sustainable. You can deposit in one payment or in instalments, subject to the scheme’s annual minimum and maximum. Before choosing a monthly amount, account for rent, EMIs, insurance premiums, school fees and emergency savings. A contribution that forces you to borrow on a credit card defeats the purpose of disciplined saving. If your income is irregular, you may prefer to make contributions when cash is available while keeping track of the annual minimum and deadline.

How Much Should You Invest Monthly to Reach a Goal? A Reverse SIP Guide
A guide to reverse SIP calculations, future-value assumptions, time horizons and return sensitivity, using illustrative rupee examples rather than forecasts.

A reverse SIP calculation takes a target goal and calculates what you would need to contribute regularly to achieve this. Essentially you’re calculating how much you’d need to contribute each month to achieve your chosen target amount, based on your assumptions. This is a very useful tool to help you plan how you will achieve your goal but is not a prediction. The accuracy of the calculation will depend on how well you know how long you’ll be contributing for, when you’ll be contributing and what rate of return you’re assuming.

This can be useful to make a big goal feel more tangible. By putting a number and date on your goal (e.g. future education costs, a future purchase you want to make or long term savings) you can understand what you’re aiming for. However, you may need to factor in inflation for your goal amount and increase your contribution depending on changes in your income. Using a calculator can also help you have a discussion around your assumptions.

## Know your goal

Start by writing down what the money is for and when you’ll need it. A goal such as ‘build wealth’ is too vague. You need to be specific with your goal. You could write ‘save an illustrative ₹8 lakh in 8 years’. This gives you something to work with but your target amount may not be exactly what you’ll need to pay in the future. If you’re saving for a future expense you may want to factor in that the price could go up.

## How much do you currently have?

If you currently have some savings then your total to build will be less than if you have nothing. However, don’t include emergency savings or money for another commitment. Your goal should reflect how much really can be allocated towards it.

## Maths behind the calculation

Most reverse SIP calculators use a future value calculation. This assumes you’re making regular monthly contributions, growing at a steady rate (converted to a monthly rate). This gives you an approximation of how much you’ll have. Most calculators will assume you’re contributing at the end of each month. This will slightly alter your answer.

Investment returns will not be a straight line. Investments linked to the market will fluctuate and your returns may be affected by charges and tax. Using a steady rate calculation helps you to see your assumptions and compare them. However, it won’t reflect every market scenario. Check how the calculator handles compounding, contribution dates, initial capital and charges.

## Example in rupees

Let’s say your goal is to have an illustrative ₹8,00,000 in 8 years. This calculator may ask you to try several rates of return. The higher the rate you assume the less you’ll need to contribute each month. These are just hypothetical numbers. The lower the rate you assume the higher you’ll need to contribute each month. This is purely maths and doesn’t mean you can pick a higher rate of return to make the monthly figure look good.

It’s best to run at least three scenarios. One with a conservative rate of return, one with a moderate rate (just to compare) and one with a higher rate of return to see how sensitive your goal is. All results should be noted as illustrative. If you’re only achieving your goal with the highest rate of return then your goal may be quite uncertain. Just because you’re contributing an amount that looks affordable doesn’t mean you’ll achieve your goal.

## Time

The longer you contribute for the more time your monthly contributions will have to build up and earn returns. This will often mean you’ll be able to achieve your goal with a lower monthly contribution. If you’re contributing for a shorter period of time you’ll generally need to contribute more as there will be fewer contributions and less compounding.

Check when your goal is. An 8 year goal is not the same as an 8 year and 6 month goal. If you’re contributing monthly the number of contributions and dates will affect how much you’ll need. Also check if your first contribution will be immediately or in one month. Don’t compare two calculators unless they have the same assumptions.

## Sensitivity

Having one rate of return can give you a false sense of security. Increasing the rate by a little may mean your contribution decreases a lot and looks good. However, you don’t get to choose what happens in the market. Equity values could decrease, debt investments could have credit or interest rate risk and different funds will behave differently. Inflation will also affect how much you’ll have.

A useful way of seeing how sensitive your goal is is to change one assumption at a time. Start by keeping your goal and time frame the same but trying different rates of return. Next keep your rate the same but shorten the time frame. Finally think about increasing your goal as the cost may increase. This isn’t to give you a perfect prediction but to show you what your goal depends on the most.

## Not a fixed contribution

Most basic reverse SIP calculations assume you’ll be contributing the same amount each month. In reality your salary could increase, decrease or be interrupted. Some households may be able to increase their contributions each year whereas others may need to decrease during times of unemployment or family expenditure. If you’re planning to increase your contributions in steps you’ll need to do a different calculation. The increases should be realistic.

If you’re reviewing your plan yearly you should check how much you’re contributing. If you’re missing out on contributions this can impact how much you have at the end, especially if it’s early on and you’ve lost out on compounding. Adding extra later may help but it will depend on how much you’re adding, when and what your actual returns are. Don’t use a calculator as a replacement for checking your plan against your cash flow.

## Inflation

A goal of ₹8 lakh in the future may seem like a lot now but after several years of inflation it may not be as much. If your goal is related to education, healthcare or housing make sure you’re estimating how much it will cost in the future. When making assumptions around inflation make sure to label them as assumptions and review them using credible data when updating this article.

Inflation is not the same as investment returns. A nominal return is how much your investment has increased in rupees. A real return takes into consideration how much your purchasing power has changed after inflation. Whilst your calculator may be mathematically accurate you may not have enough to buy the products/services you wanted. Your goal should reflect what it will be used for in the real world.

## Understanding your answer

Your answer will give you a rough idea of how much you’ll need to contribute each month. Think about whether this fits with your essential expenditure, debt repayments and cash buffer. If not you should consider changing your goal, time frame or contributions. Don’t assume you’ll get a better return by being an aggressive investor. Some goals can be delayed or come from multiple sources whereas others will be on a fixed date. You’ll need to make practical decisions based on your goal and household.

## The investment

A calculator won’t tell you what mutual fund or investment to use. Your risk, liquidity, charges, tax and when you need the money will all impact whether it’s suitable for your goal. Just because you’re contributing for a longer period of time doesn’t mean all high risk investments will be suitable. You may need to go for something with less volatility but it may not keep up with inflation.

## Common mistakes

Don’t mix up annual percentage returns and monthly rates. Make sure to check how the calculator converts these. Don’t forget to include any initial lump sum. Don’t assume you’ll definitely have the amount shown. Don’t forget to include costs.

Don’t be tempted to use a calculator that gives a very specific figure in rupees. Make sure you understand what the inputs are.

Setting a goal based on an unrealistic contribution amount. It may be more honest to start with a lower recurring contribution that fits within your household budget. If you have a large contribution amount but pause it after a few months this may not be the best approach. If your income, family commitments, cost of goal or date changes make sure to review your plan.

## Conclusion

Reverse SIP planning will help you see how much you may need to contribute to achieve your future goal based on your assumptions. It’s useful to understand how your goal amount, time frame, contribution and sensitivity to returns will impact your goal. It’s not a guarantee and your real investment journey won’t be as straightforward as a formula. Try several scenarios, factor in inflation and costs and make sure you understand the assumptions made by the calculator.

## Goal worksheet

Start by writing down your goal amount, when you’ll need the money, how much you’ve already set aside and how much you can contribute each month without borrowing. Note down the assumptions you made around your returns and when the calculator assumes you’ll be making deposits. Write down your inflation assumptions separately and if you plan to increase your contributions each year. This will help you see why you may be getting a disappointing result based on your goal, time frame or contribution.

If your goal changes make sure to review your worksheet. If your course fee has increased you may need to update your goal. If your salary has increased you may be able to increase your contributions. If your income is uncertain you may need to reduce your contribution schedule. All changes should be made honestly.

## Buffer

If your goal is calculated to the last rupee you’ll have no buffer for returns not being as high as assumed, missing out on contributions or the cost increasing unexpectedly. This can be done by increasing your goal amount or reducing your return assumption. How much of a buffer you should have will depend on your goal and household. There is no one percentage that will guarantee your investment.

The most useful thing a calculator can do is show you how fragile your goal is. If your goal looks unachievable with a small change in your assumptions this is useful to know early on.

## Turn the calculator result into a plan you can maintain

A reverse SIP calculation is a starting estimate. Before setting up a debit, compare the suggested monthly amount with your actual surplus after essential spending, debt payments and planned annual bills. If the amount is too high, do not simply reduce your emergency savings or skip insurance to make the calculation work. Change one of the assumptions instead: extend the time horizon, reduce the goal, add an initial lump sum if you genuinely have one, or plan to increase contributions as income grows.

It is useful to run at least three scenarios. A conservative case can use a lower assumed return, the base case can use your central planning assumption, and an optimistic case can show what happens if markets perform better. These are not predictions or probability ranges. They simply show how sensitive the monthly contribution is to the inputs. Never present the optimistic case as the amount someone should rely on.

## Include inflation and the date of the goal

## Revisit the plan when real life changes

SEBI Makes Direct Mutual Fund Plans Default: What Investors in India Need to Know
From 1st November 2026, Direct Mutual Fund plans are the default option on AMCs' digital platforms. Learn what this means for investors in India.

As of 1st November 2026, Direct Mutual Fund plans are now the default option available on AMCs' digital platforms. If you wish to invest in Regular Mutual Fund plans, you should be made aware of the higher expense ratios.

This doesn't mean they've been banned, or that you'll get better returns, it simply means that if you're investing on an AMC's digital platform you'll see the Direct Mutual Fund option as the default. Here's what you need to know as an investor.

## What's changed from 1st November?

The change was announced by SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on 28th October. This means if you're investing via a digital platform of an AMC (their website or app) you'll see the Direct Plan as the default. You'll still be able to invest in a Regular Plan, however you will need to be made aware of the higher expense ratio.

This announcement is regarding the digital platforms of AMCs. Not all banks, distributor apps or 3rd party platforms will need to change. However, do take note of which plan you're viewing.

## Direct Plan vs Regular Plan

Most Mutual Fund schemes will have both Direct and Regular options. These are both part of the same scheme, so will have the same underlying portfolio and fund manager. The key difference between them is how they're distributed.

### Direct Plan

A Direct Plan is bought directly from the Mutual Fund House. As you're not paying any distributor fees this will normally have a lower expense ratio than the Regular Plan. This could be the right option for those who can understand the risk in the fund, pick the right schemes for them and keep track of their investments. However, they may also pay for professional advice separately.

### Regular Plan

A Regular Plan is bought via a distributor/intermediary. As there are distribution fees involved this will generally have a higher expense ratio. This isn't necessarily a bad thing. Some investors like having support with their transactions, understanding the products and having support during volatile times. Consider if you're getting value for money.

## What is the expense ratio?

The expense ratio is the amount of money charged regularly to manage your Mutual Fund scheme. This gets added to the Net Asset Value (NAV) of your scheme.

The lower the expense ratio the less of the scheme you'll have to pay for. Over a long period this could mean you have more money invested into your scheme due to lower costs. If you're earning the same pre-expense returns from both versions of the fund, then the Direct Plan will generally have a higher net return due to the low expense ratio.

This doesn't guarantee a better investment. Both schemes will have the same risks. However, the costs won't help you avoid any drops in the market, poor asset allocation or wrong fund.

## Is Direct always better?

No. Whilst having a lower expense ratio is an important factor to consider,

A Direct Plan may be suitable if you understand what fund category you're investing in, know what the risk is, what the objective is, what the time frame is and what the asset allocation is. Also if you're happy to review your investments.

A Regular Plan may be helpful if you need support with picking your funds. Make sure you understand how your distributor is being paid and what services they're providing. Just because they're charging a fee doesn't mean they'll give you good advice or better returns. Consider how much you can manage yourself and if you need the support.

## What if I'm already invested in a Regular Plan?

You won't automatically be switched to a Direct Plan. Regular Plans haven't been removed. Don't feel the need to switch.

However, switching to a Direct Plan is usually seen as a switch. This means you'll have to redeem your units and purchase them again. This could mean you pay capital gain tax. You may also pay an exit load depending on your scheme and how long you've held the units.

**Before switching consider:**

- **What is the expense ratio?** Compare the expense ratios of the Direct Plan and Regular Plan. This is for the exact same scheme.
- **Will I pay capital gains?** Work out if switching will cause you to pay capital gain.
- **Will I pay an exit load?** Check what the exit load is for your scheme and how long you've held your units.
- **Am I getting value for money?** Do you currently get any useful support from your distributor?
- **Is this the right scheme for me?** Make sure the scheme and asset allocation suits your financial goals.

If you have a large portfolio or complex tax situation you may want to speak to a qualified tax professional or appropriately registered investment adviser.

## Things to check before investing

**Make sure:**

- You're investing in the correct plan type.
- You're investing in the correct scheme. Don't invest in two similar schemes.
- Compare the expense ratios. Check the latest Total Expense Ratio (TER) for your scheme.
- Understand the risk. Read through the scheme information and understand what the risk level is.
- Consider your goals. Make sure the fund suits your time frame and asset allocation.
- Know who's advising you. Do you get any services from your distributor? Are you getting registered investment advice? Or just access to transactions?
- Keep a record. Keep a copy of your confirmation and periodically check your consolidated portfolio statement.

## What does this mean for the Mutual Fund industry in India?

This puts more of a focus on showing the costs of your investment clearly. Having a default option can impact what you choose, especially if you're new to investing in Mutual Funds and didn't know there were two options. This means people who want to invest without using a distributor may not accidentally choose an option with a higher cost. It may also put more focus on asking your distributor what services they provide and how they charge.

However, just because it's easier to access doesn't mean you'll understand how to invest. You will still need to understand the risks, diversification, costs, time frames and difference between execution and personal advice. Distributors may need to show the value they provide and AMCs should ensure they're providing clear disclosures.

## FAQs

1. **Are Regular Mutual Fund Plans no longer available from November 2026?**  
   No. They're still available. However, Direct Mutual Fund Plans will now be the default option on AMCs' digital platforms. You'll need to be made aware of the higher expense ratios if you choose to invest in Regular Mutual Fund Plans.

2. **Will my current Regular plan automatically be switched to a Direct plan?**  
   No. You won't be automatically switched. Take a look at your current holdings and consider the tax and exit load implications.

3. **Do Direct and Regular Plans invest in different stocks?**  
   No. Both the Direct and Regular options will have the same underlying portfolio and fund manager. The main difference is how they're distributed and the expense ratios.

4. **Is a Direct Plan suitable for everyone?**  
   Not necessarily. It may be suitable for those who can pick and monitor their funds. However, if you need regular support you may appreciate the support from your distributor. Just make sure you understand the cost.

5. **Where can I find the expense ratio for a Mutual Fund?**  
   Check the scheme disclosures from the AMC. Also check the Total Expense Ratio information from AMFI. Compare the Direct and Regular options for the same scheme. Check the latest disclosure.

## What an investor should check on the transaction screen

A default option is a starting point in an app, not a recommendation for your circumstances. Before confirming a purchase, check the exact scheme name, plan type, option (growth or IDCW), amount, bank mandate and the account in which units will be held. Similar scheme names can refer to different plans or options. Save the transaction confirmation and later verify that the units appear in the correct folio or account statement.

If you are comparing a Direct Plan and a Regular Plan of the same scheme, look at the expense ratio and understand what service is included in the route you choose. What is the expense ratio?

The expense ratio is the amount of money charged regularly to manage your Mutual Fund scheme. This gets added to the Net Asset Value (NAV) of your scheme.

The lower the expense ratio the less of the scheme you’ll have to pay for. Over a long period this could mean you have more money invested into your scheme due to lower costs. However, switching to a Direct Plan is usually seen as a switch. This means you’ll have to redeem your units and purchase them again. This could mean you pay capital gain tax. You may also pay an exit load depending on your scheme and how long you’ve held the units.
